title: Inheritance
intro: Inheritance lets a new class absorb the attributes and methods of an existing class and add its own (an is-a relationship). It is the base for polymorphism (Chapter 5), and for many quiz questions on constructors, access modifiers, final, abstract and interfaces.

cards.title: Inheritance is an is-a relationship
cards.body:
Inheritance lets you **derive a new class from an existing one**. The subclass **absorbs** the superclass's attributes and behaviours, then **adds** new ones.
Test it by saying it aloud: "a Student **is a** Person" makes sense, so Student can extend Person.
The superclass is the **generalisation**; the subclasses are **specialisations**.

cards.title: extends, and what is (not) inherited
cards.body:
A subclass is declared with `extends`. A Java class can extend **only one** class.
The subclass inherits the parent's members, **except** that `private` members can't be used by name, and **constructors are never inherited**.

cards.title: The hierarchy tree, and Object at the root
cards.body:
Classes form a tree. Going **up** is more general, going **down** is more specific. Disc extends Circle, so Shape is an **indirect** superclass of Disc.
If a class has no `extends`, it silently extends **java.lang.Object**. So every class inherits Object's methods, such as `toString()`, `equals(Object)` and `getClass()`.

cards.title: super: two different uses
cards.body:
**1. `super(args)`** inside a constructor calls the **parent's constructor**. It must be the **first statement**.
**2. `super.method()`** inside a method calls the **parent's version** of an overridden method. This is how the slides' Disc reuses Circle's `print()` and `findArea()`.
keypoints: `super(...)`: parent constructor, first line only
`super.m()`: parent's version of m()
Without `super.`, calling print() inside print() would call itself

cards.title: Constructor chaining: the parent part is built first
cards.body: `new Disc(...)` first calls Disc's constructor, and its **first** action is `super(...)`, which goes to Circle, then to Shape, then to Object. The calls go **down** the chain, and the bodies **finish from the top**, so the parent part of the object is always initialised before the child part.

cards.title: The implicit super()
cards.body:
If a constructor does **not** start with `super(...)` or `this(...)`, the compiler secretly inserts `super();`, a call to the parent's **no-argument** constructor.
If a class has no constructor at all, Java gives it a default one, which also calls `super()`.

cards.title: Overloading vs overriding
cards.body:
**Overloading**: same method name, **different parameter list** (number or types). Example: `findMin(int,int)` and `findMin(double,double)`. Not really about inheritance.
**Overriding**: a subclass redefines an inherited method with the **same signature and return type**. Two styles: **refinement** (call `super.m()` and add more) and **replacement** (rewrite completely).

cards.title: Resolving a method call
cards.body: When a method is called on an object, Java searches for it **starting at the object's own class**, then moves to its immediate superclass, and continues **up** the tree until a match is found. If none is found, it is an error (caught by the compiler).

cards.title: Visibility modifiers
cards.body:
**public**: visible everywhere. **private**: only inside the class itself. **protected**: the class, **any class in the same package**, and **subclasses** ("stay in the family"). **No modifier** (package access): the class and the same package only.
UML symbols: `+` public, `#` protected, `~` package, `-` private.

cards.title: final classes and final methods
cards.body:
**final method**: cannot be overridden in a subclass.
**final class**: cannot be extended (no subclasses), so all of its methods are effectively final. Example: `String`.
The reasons the slides give: **security** (behaviour can't be changed by subclasses) and **efficiency** (the call can be bound at compile time).

cards.title: Abstract classes
cards.body:
A superclass that is **too general to create objects from** (what does a plain "Figure" look like?) is made `abstract`. An **abstract method** has **no body**, only a signature followed by `;`. Each concrete subclass **must implement** every abstract method, or it must be declared abstract too.
UML: italic name or `{abstract}`. Mermaid shows `<<abstract>>` and a `*` after abstract methods.

classDiagram

<<abstract>>
-String color
+getColor() String
+findArea()* double
+print()* void
}
class Circle {
-double radius
+findArea() double
+print() void
}
class Rectangle {
-double width
-double height
+findArea() double
+print() void
}
Figure <|-- Circle
Figure <|-- Rectangle
keypoints: Cannot `new` an abstract class, but it can have constructors and fields
A class with any abstract method must itself be abstract
Concrete class = no abstract methods left

cards.title: Interfaces (Java's answer to multiple inheritance)
cards.body:
Java does **not** allow a class to extend two classes. Instead, a class can **implement many interfaces**. As the slides present it, an interface contains **only abstract methods and constants** (`static final`). A class that implements it **promises** to code every method, otherwise it must be abstract.
An interface can `extends` another interface. A class implementing the derived interface must then code the methods of **both**.
cards.diagram:
classDiagram
class INameable {
<<interface>>
+name() String
}
INameable <|.. Person
INameable <|.. Pet
INameable <|.. Ship
cards.after: The dashed arrow with a hollow head means **implements** (realisation). Interfaces suit **unrelated** classes that share a behaviour (a Person, a Pet and a Ship all have a name).
keypoints: `extends` ONE class, `implements` MANY interfaces (extends comes first)
Interface methods are implicitly public abstract; its fields are public static final
(Slides say only abstract methods. Java 8+ also allows default and static methods.)

cards.body: Both **cannot be instantiated** with `new`, and both are used as types for references. The differences are below.

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.body:
1. Thinking **constructors are inherited**. They are not; the child must call them with `super(...)`.
2. Forgetting the **implicit super()**. If the parent has only `Parent(int)`, a child constructor without `super(5)` fails to compile.
3. Putting `super(...)` **after** another statement. It must be first.
4. Thinking `protected` means "subclasses only". It **also includes the same package**.
5. Mixing up **overload** (different parameters) and **override** (same signature).
6. Writing `new` on an abstract class or an interface.
7. `class A implements B extends C`: the order is wrong. `extends` comes first.
keypoints: Constructors: not inherited, chained by super()
protected is wider than package access
